reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Approved canonical concept synthesized from 0 legacy articles and blogs.

concept.tagline: Coordinating mutually exclusive access across independent processes using time-bounded leases and monotonic fencing tokens.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of distributed locking—from why single-node mutexes fail over a network to how production systems combine leases, watchdogs, and fencing tokens.

spark.summary: Distributed locking coordinates mutually exclusive access to a shared resource across independent processes that share no memory, using a network-accessible lease store such as Redis, etcd, or ZooKeeper.
spark.keyTakeaway: A distributed lock is only a time-bounded lease—without monotonic fencing tokens verified by the downstream storage engine, GC pauses or network partitions will still cause split-brain corruption.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** On a single machine, a `pthread_mutex` or Java `synchronized` block works because all threads share one kernel, one memory space, and one hardware clock. Across multiple servers, there is no shared memory.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Distributed Lock State Machine (UNLOCKED -> LEASED -> EXPIRED / STALE); How GC Pauses Break Leases — And How Fencing Tokens Stop Stale Writes (Worker A -> etcd / Lock -> Worker B -> Fenced DB); 3-Node etcd Raft Lock Cluster + Fenced PostgreSQL Store (etcd Leader -> etcd Follower 1 -> etcd Follower 2 -> Fenced Postgres).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choosing a locking mechanism means choosing your failure model. In production payment and inventory pipelines, teams pair an **etcd Lease** (or ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znode) with **storage-enforced fencing**.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Distributed locking is rarely an end in itself—it is a building block inside high-concurrency system designs.

learningJourney.title: What is Distributed Locking
learningJourney.explanation:
On a single machine, a `pthread_mutex` or Java `synchronized` block works because all threads share one kernel, one memory space, and one hardware clock. Across multiple servers, there is no shared memory. A **distributed lock** is a **time-bounded lease** stored in an external coordination service (such as Redis, etcd, or ZooKeeper) that grants one caller temporary exclusive permission to act on a resource key.

Every safe distributed lock has four fields: a **resource key** (`lock:invoice:77`), a **globally unique owner token** (`uuid-a`, so only the holder can release it), a **TTL / lease duration** (`PX 30000`, so a crashed holder does not deadlock the cluster forever), and—for correctness-critical writes—a **monotonic fencing token** (`revision = 412`).

sectionDiagram.title: Distributed Lock State Machine
sectionDiagram.summary: A lock never stays held forever: either the owner atomically releases it with its UUID, or the TTL expires and a new monotonic token is issued.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Distributed Locking works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Distributed Locking (and why naive locks fail)
learningJourney.explanation: When multiple stateless workers process queues, cron jobs, or checkout requests concurrently, two workers can read the same state (`stock = 1` or `invoice = UNPAID`) and both execute an irreversible side effect—double-charging a credit card or overselling the last item. Even if you add a lock, **asynchronous networks and stop-the-world GC pauses** break naive mutual exclusion: Worker A can freeze after acquiring a 10 s lock, wake up at 15 s believing it still holds the lock, and overwrite Worker B's work.

sectionDiagram.title: How GC Pauses Break Leases — And How Fencing Tokens Stop Stale Writes
sectionDiagram.summary: Mutual exclusion over an unreliable network is only safe when the storage layer rejects writes carrying a fencing token older than the highest token seen.

ideas.title: Efficiency Locks vs. Correctness Locks
ideas.description: Use an efficiency lock (like single-node Redis or Redlock) when an occasional duplicate execution only wastes CPU or money. Use a correctness lock with monotonic fencing tokens (etcd/ZooKeeper + storage check) when duplicate writes corrupt financial or inventory state.

ideas.title: The Slow-vs-Dead Ambiguity
ideas.description: A lock service cannot tell whether a silent client crashed or is merely paused in GC. That is why every lock must be a finite lease rather than an indefinite hold.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Distributed Locking under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where Distributed Locking is used (and where to avoid it)
learningJourney.explanation: Distributed locks belong at **coarse-grained coordination boundaries**, not on every database row. They shine when coordinating external side effects that lack native compare-and-swap primitives, or when electing a single active controller.

learningJourney.title: How Distributed Locks are acquired, renewed, and released
learningJourney.explanation:
Safe lock management requires atomic primitives at every step of the lifecycle:

1. **Atomic Acquisition**: Never run `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE`—a crash between the two creates an eternal lock. Always use `SET lock:sku:4829 <uuid> NX PX 30000`.
2. **Watchdog / Lease Renewal**: If work can outlive the initial TTL, run a background daemon (e.g., Redisson's watchdog) that extends the TTL at `TTL / 3` intervals—and **aborts local work** if renewal fails.
3. **Atomic Compare-and-Delete Release**: Never issue a blind `DEL lock:sku:4829`. If your lease expired during a pause, `DEL` will delete another worker's active lock. Execute a server-side Lua script that checks `GET == owner_uuid` before deleting.
4. **Bounded Retries with Jitter**: Contending callers must back off exponentially with full jitter instead of spinning in a tight `while (!acquire())` loop.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```lua
-- Atomic release in Redis: delete ONLY if the caller still owns the token
if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("del", KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end
```

```sql
-- Storage-side fencing token validation (PostgreSQL)
UPDATE ledger_accounts
SET balance_cents = balance_cents - :amount,
    last_fence_token = :fence_token
WHERE account_id = :account_id
  AND last_fence_token < :fence_token;
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Redlock vs. Consensus (etcd/ZK) vs. OCC
learningJourney.explanation: Choosing a locking mechanism means choosing your failure model. **Redlock** deploys $N = 5$ independent Redis masters and requires acquiring $\ge 3$ within `TTL - elapsed - clock_drift`. It tolerates up to 2 node crashes without disk fsync, but relies on bounded wall-clock assumptions and emits no monotonic fencing token. **etcd** (Raft) and **ZooKeeper** (Zab) persist state via quorum consensus and emit monotonic `revision` / `zxid` numbers, trading higher write latency (5–20 ms) for linearizable safety.

benefits: Linearizable quorum + monotonic `revision`/`zxid` fencing tokens; immune to wall-clock jumps.
costs: 5–20 ms write latency (disk fsync + quorum RTT); heavier cluster operations.

benefits: Sub-2 ms in-memory latency; survives 2 of 5 Redis node failures without async-replica loss.
costs: No monotonic fencing token; vulnerable to NTP clock steps and long GC pauses.

benefits: Zero external lock store; scales horizontally under low contention.
costs: Wastes work on conflicts under high contention; cannot guard non-transactional external APIs.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Fenced etcd Lock + Storage Guard
learningJourney.explanation: In production payment and inventory pipelines, teams pair an **etcd Lease** (or ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znode) with **storage-enforced fencing**. The lock service provides the monotonic `revision`, and the authoritative database rejects any write whose `fence_token <= last_fence_token`.

cards.label: Step 1 — Lease + Token
cards.detail: Worker acquires an etcd lease; Raft consensus commits and returns monotonic revision 413.

cards.label: Step 2 — Watchdog KeepAlive
cards.detail: Background gRPC stream renews the lease every TTL/3; if renewal drops, the worker aborts its critical section.

cards.label: Step 3 — Storage Fencing
cards.detail: Postgres atomically checks last_fence_token < 413 on UPDATE, neutralizing any zombie worker with token 412.

sectionDiagram.summary: Consensus issues the monotonic token; the database enforces it.

knowledgeCheck.question: Worker A acquires a 10 s Redis lock, enters a 15 s GC pause, and wakes up while Worker B now holds the lock. Which mechanism guarantees Worker A's delayed database write cannot corrupt Worker B's update?

options.text: Using a Lua compare-and-delete script on unlock
options.feedback: Lua compare-and-delete only protects unlock—Worker A still executes its stale database write before calling unlock.

options.text: Monotonic fencing tokens validated by the database on write
options.feedback: Correct: the database rejects Worker A's write because its fencing token is lower than Worker B's committed token.

options.text: Increasing the Redis TTL from 10 s to 30 s
options.feedback: Longer TTLs reduce probability but cannot eliminate unbounded GC pauses or network delays—and they slow down crash recovery.
